strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear desiderata (D1-D3) and systematic comparison of existing methods
Principled theoretical foundation combining nuclear norm with first-order optimization analysis and rank-based diversity interpretation (Lemma 3.1)
Clever computational design using bilinear factorization (Theorem 3.2) reducing complexity from O(NVd) to O((N+V)d log(NV)) while preserving Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks and two model sizes with proper baselines, ablations, and sensitivity analysis
Consistent SOTA results outperforming GREATS across all benchmarks (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B MMLU: 63.34% vs 58.19%)
Successfully achieves all three design goals: no external resources, no validation set, no reference model
Clear presentation with intuitive explanations and helpful visualizations
weaknesses: SVD computation overhead for nuclear norm calculation inadequately addressed—acknowledged as 'non-negligible' for long sequences but not thoroughly investigated; approximate methods reportedly degrade performance without quantification
Efficiency gains are more modest than claimed—18-23% throughput improvements on some benchmarks, and UDS slower than full dataset in some cases; wall-clock time analysis missing

Requires substantial dataset-specific tuning: selection ratios vary dramatically across datasets (Qwen-2.5-7B uses 12.5%-50%) and optimal α values vary 3-4x (Table 6), undermining 'practical' and 'automatic' claims
Theoretical justification for optimization utility relies on first-order Taylor approximation with no convergence analysis; Figure 2 shows noisy correlation without rigorous guarantees
Nuclear norm serves as proxy for both utility and diversity—conflates distinct concepts; a sample could be high-utility but low-diversity (repetitive but challenging)
Limited scope: only evaluates supervised fine-tuning with LoRA (rank=8) and batch size 8; scalability to full fine-tuning and larger batches unclear
Missing ablations on distance metric choice, memory buffer strategies, and systematic analysis of failure modes
Code unavailable (blank in abstract); reproducibility would benefit from provided implementation
Comparison with GREATS may be unfair—GREATS requires validation set while UDS requires α/ratio tuning, different types of external knowledge
Modest practical impact: accuracy improvements of 3-7% over GREATS are meaningful but not transformative; efficiency gains limited

strengths: Well-motivated problem with three clear desiderata (D1-D3) addressing genuine limitations of existing online batch selection methods
Novel use of nuclear norm to jointly capture optimization utility and intra-sample diversity, with strong empirical validation (Spearman correlation >0.8 in Figures 2-3)

Efficient technical design avoiding external resources: logits-based scoring without gradient computation, clever structured bilinear projection (Theorem 3.2) reducing storage from ~74GB to ~1.2GB with Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 benchmarks, 2 models, consistent improvements (+5.15% on MMLU vs GREATS, faster than full-dataset training), extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses across diverse settings (Table 10-14)
Practical applicability: no requirement for reference models or validation sets, plug-and-play integration with SFT pipeline, LoRA-compatible
Reproducibility: clear pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed hyperparameters and experimental configuration, honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Theoretical foundation relies entirely on first-order Taylor approximation (Eq. 5-8) without analysis of approximation validity across training phases; rank-diversity relationship in Figure 3 shows correlation but lacks rigorous causal proof

SVD computation overhead acknowledged but unresolved: randomized SVD rejected for 'loss in precision' without quantitative analysis; no breakdown of SVD time as percentage of total training time, raising scalability concerns for long sequences and large models

Hyperparameter tuning significantly reduces practical applicability: trade-off factor α varies 1-7×10⁻³ across datasets/models without principled selection method; data selection fractions vary 12.5%-50%, making it unclear if improvements stem from the algorithm or dataset-specific tuning

Experimental design concerns: non-uniform data selection fractions (Table 5) may confound results; RHO-Loss uses suboptimal surrogate reference model; GREATS penalized for requiring validation set despite being designed for it; LoRA-only primary experiments may not generalize to full fine-tuning

Limited generalization analysis: all tasks are instruction-following QA; method shows notably smaller improvements on instruction-tuned models (2.2% vs 5.15% on base models); scalability to 70B+ models undemonstrated; no exploration of failure modes or edge cases
FIFO buffer strategy not critical (ablation Table 7 shows equivalence to alternatives); buffer size M=1024 appears 4× larger than saturation point (~256), suggesting suboptimal design choices

Statistical rigor: no significance testing performed; some improvements marginal with overlapping error bars; nuclear norm vs. cheaper alternatives (Frobenius norm, top-k singular values) not compared
